answers.brief_reasoning: Each 30 s, [A] is multiplied by the same factor, 0.7634, which is what first-order decay looks like. If you plot ln[A] against time, the points fall on a straight line with slope -k. Plots of [A] or 1/[A] against time are curved.

answers.brief_reasoning: For a first-order reaction, t1/2 = ln2/k = 0.693/0.00900. It does not depend on the starting concentration.

At a higher temperature, molecules move faster, so they collide more often. A larger fraction of collisions also has energy at or above the activation energy. More effective collisions per unit time means a faster rate, so k is larger.
In an elementary step, the rate law follows from the molecularity. Rate = k[A] (first order in A) matches a step in which one A particle reacts: A → products.

answers.brief_reasoning: There are 5 electrons in a 2:2:1 pattern, which fills 1s, 2s and 2p. The energies match boron's known PES values.

By Coulomb's law, attraction grows as the charges grow and as the distance shrinks (F ∝ q1q2/r²). The 1s electrons are closest to the nucleus and have no inner electrons shielding them, so they feel the full +5 charge. That makes them the hardest to remove, so they have the highest binding energy.
answers.final_answer: The 1s electrons are closest to the nucleus and unshielded, so they feel the strongest attraction and have the highest binding energy.

answers.brief_reasoning: Carbon is 1s2 2s2 2p2, so its valence peaks are a 2s peak of height 2 and a 2p peak of height 2. Carbon has one more proton, but the added electron goes into the same n=2 shell, so the inner shielding is the same. The effective nuclear charge is therefore higher and the electrons are at about the same distance. That means stronger attraction and higher binding energies.
answers.final_answer: Sketch a 2s peak of height 2 at slightly above 1.36 MJ/mol (about 1.7) and a 2p peak of height 2 at slightly above 0.8 MJ/mol (about 1.1). Both valence peaks appear at higher binding energy than X's, because carbon has a larger effective nuclear charge with the same shell and shielding.

answers.brief_reasoning: The first ionization energy is the binding energy of the lowest-energy peak, which is the 2p electron. Carbon's 2p peak sits at a higher binding energy (about 1.09) than boron's (0.80). This is because carbon's greater nuclear charge, with the same shielding, holds its 2p electrons more strongly.
answers.final_answer: Larger: carbon's 2p peak appears at a higher binding energy than boron's 0.80 MJ/mol.

answers.brief_reasoning: C is in the center with 4 single bonds to H, which uses all 8 valence electrons (4 from C, 1 from each H). There are no lone pairs.
answers.final_answer: Central C with four single C–H bonds (4 shared pairs, 8 valence electrons total). No lone pairs on C.

answers.brief_reasoning: There are 4 bonding domains and 0 lone pairs around C, so the shape is tetrahedral (VSEPR).
The C–H bonds are only slightly polar. In a symmetric tetrahedron the bond dipoles cancel, so the net dipole is zero.
answers.final_answer: Nonpolar: the four C–H bond dipoles are arranged symmetrically (tetrahedral) and cancel, giving no net dipole moment.

answers.brief_reasoning: CH3OH has an O–H group, so its molecules can hydrogen bond to each other. C2H6 is nonpolar and has only London dispersion forces. The two molecules have similar molar masses (32 vs 30 g/mol), so their dispersion forces are similar.
answers.final_answer: CH3OH molecules attract each other by hydrogen bonding (through the O–H group) as well as dipole–dipole and dispersion forces. C2H6 has only London dispersion forces, and these are about the same size as in CH3OH because the molar masses are similar. Hydrogen bonds are much stronger, so more energy is needed to separate CH3OH molecules, which gives it the higher boiling point.
